#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services Survey (MARTS)
Organization/publisher: U.S. Census Bureau
Description: The U.S. Census Bureau conducts the Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services Survey (MARTS) to produce early national estimates of total and month-to-month change in sales for retail and food service establishments located in the United States. A retail establishment is one that sells merchandise to the general public (final consumers). The estimates from MARTS are released approximately ten business days after the end of the reference month and are revised one month later by estimates from the Monthly Retail Trade and Food Services Survey (MRTS). Estimates are summarized by industry classification based on the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS).

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services Survey (MARTS)
Organization/publisher: U.S. Census Bureau
Description: The U.S. Census Bureau conducts the Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services Survey (MARTS) to produce early national estimates of total and month-to-month change in sales for retail and food service establishments located in the United States. A retail establishment is one that sells merchandise to the general public (final consumers). The estimates from MARTS are released approximately ten business days after the end of the reference month and are revised one month later by estimates from the Monthly Retail Trade and Food Services Survey (MRTS). Estimates are summarized by industry classification based on the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS).

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research this dataset thoroughly. Let me start with several searches to verify the facts and gather comprehensive details.I have comprehensive information. Let me verify one historical detail about when food services were added to the survey.# Research Report: Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services Survey (MARTS)

## 1. Verification of Your Stated Information

Your information checks out against official sources. A few refinements worth noting:

- **Title/publisher**: Correct. The survey is published by the U.S. Census Bureau (Department of Commerce), specifically the Retail Indicators Branch of the Economic Directorate. The Census Bureau's own current materials sometimes shorten the name to "Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey," and the headline product is often called the "advance retail sales report" or "Advance Monthly Retail Trade Report."
- **Description**: Correct, per the Census Bureau's methodology page (census.gov/retail/marts/how_surveys_are_collected.html). The release lag is variously stated as "approximately 9–10 working/business days" after the reference month — both figures appear in official documentation.
- **One nuance**: The estimates cover **employer firms**. As of the April 2025 annual revision report, **nonemployer businesses** (firms without paid employees) were *removed* from the estimates and the time series, to align with the Annual Integrated Economic Survey (AIES). Older descriptions (and some archived pages) state that nonemployers were included via a benchmarking adjustment — that is now out of date.

---

## 2. Who Publishes It

- **Issuing agency**: U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Department of Commerce.
- **Program office**: Economic Directorate, Retail Indicators Branch.
- **OMB clearance**: The survey operates under OMB Control Number **0607-0104**, jointly with the Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MRTS); together they are called the **Monthly Retail Surveys (MRS)**. The Census Bureau periodically renews this clearance through the Paperwork Reduction Act process, with notices in the Federal Register (e.g., January 2023 and August 2025 notices requesting extensions).
- **Respondent obligation**: Voluntary (per the Federal Register supporting statements).

---

## 3. Authority and Mandate

- **Statutory authority**: **Title 13, U.S. Code, Sections 131 and 182** — these authorize the Census Bureau to conduct current surveys of business between the quinquennial economic censuses.
- **Confidentiality**: **Title 13, Section 9** requires that respondent data be kept confidential and used only for statistical purposes; Title 13 §214 and Title 18 §§3559/3571 impose criminal penalties (up to 5 years imprisonment and/or $250,000 fines) for wrongful disclosure. Data transmission is protected under the Federal Cybersecurity Enhancement Act of 2015. The Census Bureau's Disclosure Review Board applies disclosure-limitation rules so no estimate reveals an individual firm's operations.
- **Principal Federal Economic Indicator (PFEI) status**: Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services is one of roughly 35 OMB-designated PFEIs, governed by **OMB Statistical Policy Directive No. 3**. This carries concrete obligations:
  - A release schedule for the coming calendar year must be published in advance (reported to OMB by September 15);
  - Releases occur at a fixed time — **8:30 a.m. ET** — and dates/methods are set by the statistical agency, not political officials;
  - Executive Branch employees are barred from publicly commenting for **30 minutes** after release (shortened from one hour by an OMB update effective February 19, 2024);
  - Planned methodological changes must be announced at least three months in advance;
  - Pre-release access is tightly controlled (managed within Commerce by the Office of the Under Secretary for Economic Affairs).
- This PFEI status matters for preservationists and activists: it embeds the series in a formal governance framework with equity-of-access and independence protections.

---

## 4. History and Evolution

- **Origins**: The monthly retail trade estimates date to **1953**. The advance survey was developed in response to requests from government, business, and other users for an *early* read on retail activity.
- **Suspension and reinstatement**: Publication of the advance report was **suspended from roughly March 1970 to January/February 1972** because the advance estimates tracked the later monthly estimates poorly. It was resumed after the estimation procedure was modified (the link-relative approach against the larger monthly sample). The Census Bureau reports that the average absolute revision to the advance estimate is now about **two-tenths of one percent**.
- **Historical release archive**: Census maintains historic releases back to the 1950s; a handful of months are missing (May 1954, January 1956, August 1956, December 1958, January 1970, December 1973, August 1991), plus the 1970–72 gap.
- **SIC → NAICS transition**: Estimates shifted from the Standard Industrial Classification to the North American Industry Classification System around 2001–2002, which brought **food services and drinking places (NAICS 722)** into the retail trade estimates — hence the current title, "…for Retail and Food Services." Subsequent restatements: 2012 NAICS with the May 2018 annual revision; **2017 NAICS** with the benchmark report released April 25, 2025. Affected time series are restated back to the beginning of each series to preserve comparability.
- **E-commerce**: E-commerce sales of retailers are included in total monthly sales; quarterly e-commerce estimates are produced separately (from MRTS).
- **2025 nonemployer removal**: As noted above, the April 2025 annual revision removed nonemployers from the series to align with the Annual Integrated Economic Survey (AIES), which itself replaced the Annual Retail Trade Survey (ARTS).
- **Sample revisions**: The sample is re-selected roughly every 2.5–3 years to keep it representative, redistribute respondent burden, and incorporate classification updates. The current sample is ~4,800 employer firms; a prior sample was ~5,500.

---

## 5. Methodology (What a Data Scientist Should Know)

- **Design**: MARTS is a **subsample of ~4,800 employer firms** drawn from the larger **MRTS sample of ~13,000 firms**. Stratified random sampling: **36 primary industry strata**, substratified by sales size (3–12 substrata per primary stratum). Roughly **1,150 firms** are selected "with certainty" (weight = 1) because of their outsized influence; sampling weights otherwise range from 1 to ~1,000. Selection is systematic probability-proportional-to-size within strata, using the MRTS sampling weight as the size measure.
- **Universe**: Weighted and benchmarked to represent **over three million** retail and food services firms.
- **Collection**: Mail-out/mail-back (with electronic reporting options). Forms go out ~5 working days before month-end; responses due ~2 working days after month-end. Small and medium firms rotate out after about two years.
- **Estimator**: A **link-relative estimator**. For each detailed industry, the ratio of current-month to previous-month weighted sales (from units responding in both months) is multiplied by the previous month's preliminary sales estimate from the larger MRTS. Broader industry totals are sums of detailed estimates. There is **no unit-level imputation for most nonrespondents** in MARTS (except for a limited number of influential nonrespondents estimated from historical performance), which is why the link-relative is used.
- **Variance**: Estimated via the **random groups method**; published confidence intervals (e.g., ±0.4–0.5% on the month-to-month change in total sales) let users test statistical significance. A well-known caveat: the margin of error on the headline monthly change often means the change is *statistically indistinguishable from zero*.
- **Seasonal adjustment**: **X-13ARIMA-SEATS** (X-11 filter-based variant), adjusting for seasonal, holiday, and trading-day effects. Both seasonally adjusted and not-adjusted estimates are published.
- **Revision chain**: Advance estimate (MARTS, ~9–10 business days) → preliminary/final MRTS estimates (revised over the following two months) → annual benchmarking to AIES (monthly-to-annual reconciliation) → benchmarked ultimately to the **quinquennial Economic Census** of Retail Trade. This tiered structure is essential for anyone doing vintage-data or real-time-data analysis.
- **Comparability caution**: No new business "births" are added between sample redesigns, so the sample ages between re-selections — a known source of drift that sample revisions address.

---

## 6. Scope, Content, and Coverage

- **Variables**: Monthly sales (dollar value) by kind of business; month-to-month and year-over-year percent changes; seasonally adjusted and unadjusted series. No state or local geography — **national estimates only**.
- **Industry detail**: NAICS-based, from total retail and food services down through major groupings (motor vehicle and parts dealers, furniture, electronics, building materials, food and beverage stores, health and personal care, gasoline stations, clothing, sporting goods, general merchandise, nonstore retailers, food services and drinking places, etc.).
- **Related products**: MRTS (adds inventories and quarterly e-commerce), AIES (annual, formerly ARTS), Quarterly E-Commerce Report, Economic Census of Retail Trade.

---

## 7. Access, Formats, and Preservation-Relevant Facts

- **Primary release**: PDF press release plus Excel/CSV tables on census.gov/retail and the Economic Briefing Room, at 8:30 a.m. ET.
- **Machine access**: Census Bureau's **Economic Indicator data tools/API** (program code MARTS at census.gov/econ/currentdata); historical time series downloadable in bulk.
- **Third-party mirrors** (important for preservation and research):
  - **FRED** (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis): e.g., series **RSXFS** (Advance Retail Sales: Retail Trade, SA, monthly, from Jan 1992), **RSAFS** (retail + food services), plus not-adjusted variants (RSXFSN).
  - **ALFRED**: the *vintage* archive — crucial because MARTS/MRTS estimates are revised. ALFRED preserves what the data looked like at each release date, enabling real-time analysis; archived vintages begin in June 2001.
- **License**: U.S. government work — public domain (citation requested).
- **Preservation risks/considerations**:
  - Census.gov pages are periodically reorganized (URLs under /retail/marts/ have changed over time; some older material survives only at www2.census.gov archives or the bhs.econ.census.gov mirror).
  - **Revisions overwrite**: the "current" files (marts_current.pdf, current spreadsheets) are replaced each cycle; without deliberate archiving, the advance values as originally released would be lost. ALFRED and the Census "historic releases" archive mitigate this.
  - Classification breaks (SIC→NAICS 1997/2001→2012→2017) mean long time series exist in multiple vintages; preserving the restatement documentation is as important as preserving the numbers.
  - Gaps (1970–72 suspension; scattered missing months) should be documented in any preserved copy.
  - Release schedules can slip during government shutdowns (e.g., delayed releases in late 2025), another reason to capture schedules and release calendars as metadata.

---

## 8. Typical Users

Per the Census Bureau and observable usage:

- **Bureau of Economic Analysis**: key input to **GDP** estimates (personal consumption expenditures on goods) — retail sales feed the advance GDP estimate.
- **Federal Reserve Board**: anticipating economic trends and monetary policy deliberation.
- **Council of Economic Advisers / White House**: economic policy analysis.
- **Financial markets**: the 8:30 a.m. "retail sales" release is a marquee market-moving data point; futures reprice within minutes (a fact OMB itself cited in the Directive No. 3 rulemaking).
- **Businesses**: retailers, manufacturers, and logistics firms benchmarking demand and planning.
- **Academic researchers and data scientists**: consumer spending, business cycles, nowcasting, seasonal-adjustment research, real-time-data studies (using ALFRED vintages).
- **Journalists and the public**: consumer demand is roughly two-thirds of GDP, so retail sales serve as a headline barometer of household economic health.
- **State/local governments and regional planners**: as context (though no subnational detail is published).

---

## 9. Benefits to the Public

- **Timeliness**: the earliest broad-based monthly measure of U.S. consumer demand — available ~9–10 business days after month-end, well before most comparable data.
- **Macroeconomic policy**: better monetary and fiscal decisions via BEA, the Fed, and CEA use.
- **Market efficiency**: a pre-announced, simultaneous, equitable release (PFEI rules) levels the playing field for all market participants.
- **Accountability**: transparent methodology, published margins of error, announced methodological changes, and a full revision/benchmarking chain back to the Economic Census.
- **Statistical ecosystem**: anchors the retail family of statistics (MRTS inventories, e-commerce, AIES, Economic Census), enabling consistent measurement from monthly flash estimates to quinquennial benchmarks.
- **Burden-conscious design**: voluntary response, small sample relative to a 3-million-firm universe, and rotation of small firms limits burden — a model of efficient official statistics.

---

## 10. Key Facts at a Glance

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Publisher | U.S. Census Bureau (Dept. of Commerce), Retail Indicators Branch |
| Legal authority | Title 13 U.S.C. §§131, 182; confidentiality under §9 |
| OMB control no. | 0607-0104 (with MRTS, "Monthly Retail Surveys") |
| Status | OMB-designated Principal Federal Economic Indicator (Statistical Policy Directive No. 3) |
| Frequency / lag | Monthly; ~9–10 business days after reference month, 8:30 a.m. ET |
| Sample | ~4,800 employer firms (subsample of ~13,000-firm MRTS); ~1,150 certainty cases |
| History | Monthly since 1953; suspended Mar 1970–Jan/Feb 1972; NAICS since 2001–02 era; 2017 NAICS from April 2025 benchmark |
| Estimator | Link-relative; X-13ARIMA-SEATS seasonal adjustment; random-groups variance |
| Revision path | Advance (MARTS) → MRTS revisions → AIES annual benchmark → Economic Census |
| Access | census.gov PDF/Excel/API; FRED (RSXFS, RSAFS); ALFRED for vintages |
| License | Public domain (U.S. government work) |

## Sources Consulted

- Census Bureau: MARTS methodology, about-the-survey, sample revision FAQs, historical releases, current release PDFs (census.gov/retail/...)
- OMB supporting statement, OMB Control No. 0607-0104 (reginfo.gov)
- Federal Register notices (Jan 13, 2023; Aug 5, 2025; Feb 15, 2024 Directive No. 3 update)
- OMB Schedule of Release Dates for Principal Federal Economic Indicators (2024–2027)
- Department of Commerce Administrative Order 216-19 (PFEI release management)
- FRED/ALFRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (series RSXFS, RSAFS; release ID 9)

I'll research the current risk context: agency funding, staffing, shutdown-related delays, and any administration actions affecting Census economic statistics in 2025.One more check to confirm the ICR renewal status and staffing data.# Risk Assessment: Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services Survey (MARTS)

*Assessment date context: late 2025 through early 2026 events covered, including the record 43-day government shutdown (Oct 1–Nov 12, 2025), FY2026 budget cycle, and administration actions since January 2025.*

*Correction to my prior report: the current OMB control number for MARTS is **0607-0717** ("Monthly Retail Surveys," covering MARTS + MRTS); 0607-0104 was a legacy MARTS number last active around 2015.*

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence by risk level:**
- *Gone/High/Moderate*: No evidence found that any historical files have been removed from Census.gov. The Census Bureau maintains historic advance releases back to the 1950s (census.gov/retail/marts/historic_releases.html and www2.census.gov archives), including through the shutdown period (e.g., adv2509.pdf, the September 2025 release, is archived). Full historical series are also redundantly mirrored on FRED and ALFRED (St. Louis Fed), which preserve vintages back to 2001.
- *Caveat relevant to "Moderate"*: The April 2025 benchmark removed nonemployer businesses from the estimates and **restated the historical time series** — so previously published historical values that included nonemployers are no longer the "current" series, though restatement documentation and ALFRED vintages preserve the old values. This is routine benchmark practice, not data destruction.

**Assessment: No Known Issue.** Prior-year data remain accessible with no known alterations beyond documented methodological restatements, and independent mirrors (FRED/ALFRED) provide strong redundancy.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence by risk level:**
- *High Risk*: No statutory deadline missed; collection was not terminated; no cycle permanently skipped for MARTS itself.
- *Moderate Risk*: **Multiple publication dates were missed/delayed.** Due to the 43-day shutdown, the September 2025 advance report (normally ~mid-October) was released Nov 25; October on Dec 16; November on Jan 14, 2026; December on Feb 10, 2026 (Reuters, Nov 19, 2025; release PDFs stamped "Report delayed due to recent lapse in federal funding"). Related products were hit harder: the Sept/Oct/Nov advance retail **inventories** estimates (in the Advance Economic Indicators Report) were **canceled outright** (Investopedia, Dec 2025). To catch up, Census announced it was **shortening PFEI collection windows** (e.g., 10 business days of response time narrowed to 7) (gvwire.com, Dec 3, 2025). A full 2026–2027 release schedule is now published.
- *No Known Issue* (ICR leg): The ICR (OMB 0607-0717) was renewed on the normal cycle — 60-day notice Aug 5, 2025 (90 FR 37468); 30-day notice Dec 3, 2025 (90 FR 55717); **approved April 6, 2026 with expiration 04/30/2029** (reginfo.gov, ICR 202511-0607-002). No lapse.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** The ICR is active through 2029, but the typical publication dates were demonstrably missed for four consecutive monthly cycles, and sibling indicators were canceled — showing the release cadence is vulnerable to funding lapses. With further shutdown risk in the FY2026 environment, delayed (not terminated) publication is the realistic exposure.

---

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence by risk level:**
- *High Risk*: No confirmed reduction in frequency or published industry detail; every delayed MARTS release eventually appeared with full NAICS breakouts and confidence intervals.
- *Moderate Risk (emerging)*: (a) Census **temporarily compressed collection windows and processing stages** post-shutdown, acknowledging "reduced response stemming from a shorter collection window" as a risk to be mitigated (Census statement, Dec 3, 2025) — shorter response windows can depress response rates and increase revision magnitudes for a link-relative estimator with minimal imputation. (b) The **April 2025 removal of nonemployers** narrowed the conceptual coverage of the series (a deliberate alignment with AIES, documented, but a real reduction in universe coverage). (c) Agency-wide staffing losses (~15%) and a hiring freeze strain the Retail Indicators Branch's capacity. (d) Termination of the **Federal Economic Statistics Advisory Committee and Census Scientific Advisory Committee** (effective Feb 28, 2025, per 90 FR 24383) removes the external expert review channel for economic survey methodology — Reuters and Science both reported concerns this could affect data quality over time.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** Quality-in-publication is so far maintained, but there are documented, concrete emerging risks to timeliness and response quality, plus the loss of advisory oversight.

---

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence:**
- Explicit statutory authority: **13 U.S.C. §§131 and 182**, named on the ICR itself ("Authorizing Statute(s): US Code: 13 USC 131 and 182," per the reginfo.gov abstract).
- Clear programmatic use: the ICR abstract states BEA uses the data for the **National Income and Product Accounts (GDP)** and input-output benchmarks; the Federal Reserve uses retail data; the series is an OMB-designated **Principal Federal Economic Indicator** governed by Statistical Policy Directive No. 3.
- No substitute collection exists at comparable timeliness; private alternatives (e.g., card-spend panels) do not replicate the benchmarked, NAICS-structured official series.

**Assessment: No Known Issue.** This is among the most statutorily and institutionally entrenched datasets in the federal statistical system. (Note: PFEI status also functions as a protective priority — both the FY2026 budget documents and BLS/BEA justifications explicitly commit to prioritizing PFEI production.)

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence by risk level:**
- *Moderate Risk thresholds*: Census lost an estimated **~15% of staff since FY24** (American Statistical Association, "The Nation's Data at Risk," 2025) — within the 10–39% band.
- *High Risk thresholds (met on two counts)*: (a) AFGE reported **at least 1,300 employees lost** since January 2025 via deferred resignation and early retirement (GovExec, July 2025) — exceeding the rubric's 1,000-staff trigger; (b) **leadership removed** — Director Robert Santos departed early in February 2025 amid administration pressure, and as of September 2025 the bureau is led by **acting director George Cook, a political appointee** who simultaneously holds the acting Under Secretary for Economic Affairs role (NPR, Sept 19, 2025; CBPP) — a departure from the norm of a career or Senate-confirmed director.
- *Budget*: Top-line FY26 enacted ~$1.7B (driven by decennial ramp-up), but **Current Surveys and Programs cut from $329M to $319M** (~3%), and the administration's request had sought $289M (~12% cut). Current Economic Statistics held flat at $216M. Budget cuts alone do not reach the 20% trigger.
- *Additional strain*: government-wide hiring freeze; Commerce policy requiring Secretary-level approval of contracts >$100K created a 3,000+ item backlog; OIG findings of persistent field-staff vacancies.

**Assessment: High Risk.** By the rubric's explicit and/or logic, the agency exceeds the 1,000-staff-loss threshold and has experienced leadership removal. I note for calibration that the losses are Census-wide (much concentrated in decennial/demographic operations), and the retail indicators program specifically has not been documented as gutted — but the rubric's thresholds are met at the agency level.

---

## 6. Policy

**Evidence by risk level:**
- *High Risk*: No Presidential Action-driven ICR affecting MARTS; no negative policy note on the MARTS pages; no change to what MARTS collects or publishes attributable to administration priorities. Indeed, administration budget documents repeatedly commit to **prioritizing PFEIs** like retail sales.
- *Moderate Risk*: (a) The FY2026 President's Budget proposes to **reorganize BLS, BEA, and the Census Bureau into a single statistical agency at Commerce** (DOL FY2026 BIB; BEA budget submission) — a pending structural change with undefined consequences for survey programs. (b) The budget states Census "will have eliminated functions that are not statutorily mandated or core to the Bureau's mission" (COSSA analysis) — MARTS is statutorily grounded and core, so likely protected, but this signals program-elimination intent agency-wide. (c) Termination of economic-statistics advisory committees under E.O. 14217. (d) The August 2025 firing of the BLS commissioner after an unfavorable jobs report (context via NPR) demonstrates administration willingness to intervene in statistical agencies when outputs are politically inconvenient — a background risk to perceived independence, though retail sales has not been targeted.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** No changes to MARTS itself since January 2025, but there are proposed/pending structural changes and administration actions toward the statistical system that materially elevate the risk environment.

---

## Summary

| Category | Risk Level | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Historical Data Availability | **No Known Issue** | Historic releases back to the 1950s remain online; FRED/ALFRED provide redundant vintage archives; April 2025 restatement is documented benchmark practice. |
| Future Data Availability | **Moderate Risk** | Four monthly releases delayed by the 2025 shutdown (related products canceled); ICR active through 04/30/2029, so no lapse risk. |
| Data Quality | **Moderate Risk** | Temporarily shortened collection windows, nonemployer coverage removal, staffing strain, and loss of advisory committees are emerging — not yet realized — quality risks. |
| Statutory Context | **No Known Issue** | Explicit authority (13 U.S.C. §§131, 182); required GDP input; PFEI designation; no substitutes. |
| Staffing and Funding | **High Risk** | ~1,300+ staff lost agency-wide (~15%) and director departed early/replaced by political acting director; current surveys budget cut ~3% (12% proposed). |
| Policy | **Moderate Risk** | Proposed tri-agency reorganization and "eliminate non-mandated functions" language pending; MARTS itself unchanged and explicitly prioritized as a PFEI. |

**Overall interpretation**: MARTS sits in the *most protected tier* of federal statistics — statutorily grounded, GDP-critical, PFEI-designated, and explicitly prioritized in administration budget documents. The realized harms to date are shutdown-driven delays, not termination or politicization. The dominant risks are systemic to the Census Bureau (staffing, leadership instability, shutdown exposure, reorganization proposals) rather than targeted at this dataset. Preservation priority should be on **capturing each monthly vintage as released** (since revisions overwrite and schedules slip) rather than on fearing wholesale removal.
